planting.note: Direct sow or set out nursery transplants in spring into well-drained, gravelly or caliche soil in full sun; established plants resprout readily after being cut back.

directions: Tarbush is one of the defining shrubs of Chihuahuan Desert grassland and desert-scrub flats from the Trans-Pecos and southern New Mexico into northern Mexico, often forming dense colonies on heavy, calcareous soils alongside creosote and mesquite. Its small, resinous, dark green leaves give off a strong tar-like odor after rain, and in fall it produces a flush of small yellow disc flowers followed by papery, silvery seed heads that persist into winter. It tolerates extreme heat, alkaline soil, and long dry spells once established, needing only occasional deep watering its first year to root in. Use it as a structural, low-water background shrub in desert gardens, but avoid planting where livestock graze since the foliage is reported to be toxic to goats and sheep.

planting.note: Best established from nursery transplants set out in spring or fall into well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; shear lightly after bloom to keep the mound tidy.

directions: Turpentine bush grows on rocky slopes and grassland edges across the Chihuahuan and Sonoran Desert borderlands of the Southwest, forming a dense, evergreen mound of narrow, resin-scented needle-like leaves that smell of turpentine when crushed. It erupts into a blanket of small golden-yellow daisy flowers in late summer and fall, well after most desert bloomers have finished, making it a valuable late-season nectar source for bees and butterflies. It is a widely grown low-water landscape shrub across Southwestern cities, prized for its tidy rounded form, year-round green color, and minimal pruning needs once established. Give it full sun and sharp drainage, and withhold supplemental water except during the hottest, driest stretches of summer.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring onto well-drained, open soil in full sun; seed needs no stratification and self-sows readily once a planting is established.

directions: Broom snakeweed is an abundant, wiry-stemmed, rounded subshrub of Chihuahuan Desert grassland, caliche flats, and overgrazed rangeland from West Texas and southern New Mexico north through the Great Plains. It produces a dome of narrow green stems topped from midsummer through fall with masses of small yellow ray flowers that light up otherwise bare ground when little else is blooming. Deer and most grazing animals avoid it, which makes it a reliably long-lasting accent in low-maintenance xeriscape beds, and it asks for nothing beyond sun, sharp drainage, and an occasional hard cutback every few years to keep it from getting woody and sparse at the base. It needs essentially no irrigation once rooted and tolerates poor, alkaline, rocky soils that defeat most other flowering perennials.

planting.note: Nick or soak hard seed coats before direct sowing, or set out nursery transplants, in spring into well-drained soil in full sun along a wash-like low spot that collects occasional runoff.

directions: Whitethorn acacia is a thorny, multi-trunked desert-grassland shrub native to washes, bajadas, and grassy flats of the Chihuahuan and Sonoran Desert borderlands from southern New Mexico and West Texas into Mexico. Small round puffs of fragrant, pale yellow flowers appear in flushes after warm-season rains, drawing heavy bee activity, and the fine, feathery, blue-green foliage gives the plant a soft texture despite its straight white thorns. It can be grown as a loose, informal screen or trained up into a small single-trunk tree, and it tolerates heat, caliche, and long dry spells once its roots are established. Give it full sun, good drainage, and room to spread, and expect it to lose some leaves and go semi-dormant during severe drought or hard freezes, leafing back out quickly once conditions improve.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto bare, well-drained, gypsum or limestone soil so winter freeze-thaw cycles help break seed dormancy; established plants are usually short-lived but reseed readily.

directions: Fendler's penstemon is a slender, short-lived perennial of gypsum and limestone flats and grassy desert plains across the Chihuahuan Desert region of West Texas, southern New Mexico, and the Texas Panhandle into Oklahoma. Spikes of soft blue-violet, tubular flowers with contrasting reddish-purple throat markings open in spring, drawing native bees and occasionally hummingbirds, and the plant tends to behave as an annual or biennial that persists in a planting mainly by reseeding. It wants lean, mineral soil and sharp drainage rather than rich garden beds, since excess fertility and moisture shorten its already brief lifespan and invite crown rot. Let seed heads mature and shatter in place to keep a colony going from year to year, and avoid mulch or irrigation once seedlings are past their first season.
sources: Native Plant Society of New Mexico

planting.note: Direct sow or set out transplants in spring into deep, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; deep-rooted plants are slow to establish but very long-lived once they take hold.

directions: Longleaf jointfir is a stiff, pale yellow-green, leafless-stemmed shrub of sandy and gravelly desert grassland flats across the Chihuahuan Desert of West Texas, southern New Mexico, and northern Mexico, often growing alongside yuccas and soaptree stands. Its jointed, broom-like stems end in sharp spine tips, and small cone-like structures appear at the nodes in spring, followed by papery, winged seeds carried off by wind. Long used by desert peoples to brew a mild caffeine-free tea from the dried stems, it today serves gardeners mainly as an unusual, sculptural, utterly drought-proof accent for rock gardens and dry washes. It needs full sun and fast drainage, tolerates extreme heat and long rainless stretches once its deep taproot is established, and resents heavy clay or frequent watering.

planting.note: Direct sow onto bare, well-drained, rocky or gravelly soil in full sun after the soil has warmed; tiny tufts fill in slowly and establish faster from small plugs than from seed.

directions: Fluffgrass is a tiny, tufted perennial bunchgrass of gravelly desert grassland and rocky flats throughout the Chihuahuan Desert of West Texas, southern New Mexico, and adjoining deserts, often filling bare gaps between larger shrubs and cacti. Its short, curling gray-green leaves turn a soft straw color in drought and green back up within days of rain, while fuzzy, cream-colored seed heads give the whole clump a fluffy, cottony look in warm weather. Because it stays only a few inches tall and spreads slowly by short rhizomes, it works well as a low, textural filler in rock gardens, between stepping stones, or as an accent at the base of larger desert plants. It needs essentially no care beyond full sun and sharp drainage, shrugging off extreme heat and extended drought without irrigation once established.
